source:
Dear Township Council of Asbury Pines, 

I write with deep disappointment. I understand that my request to extend excavations at the Mt. Ulysses site has been denied because the land will be used for a private citizen project. One of my colleagues informs me that “bunker” construction will commence on the dig site; I certainly hope something this absurd cannot be true. 

Without exaggeration, this dig could hold the largest discoveries of our lifetime. Personally, it is everything to me. Professionally, we stand upon incredible insights into our own humanity. Insights that you, your children – all of us who share this earth – deserve to know.

大概就是他們綁走了他的女兒。我一拳捶在桌上，他嚇得說不出話。我說，我願意盡一切努力把她趕走。噢，他笑得像隻咧嘴貓。

再過幾天，我又要去他家吃晚飯了。路易，這可能就是傳說中的黃金國。這個老蠢蛋擁有鎮上最大的銀行，還有另一個正適合出嫁的女兒，以及大把鈔票……等人繼承。

祝我好運吧，老朋友。

波

source: Danny: Welcome, welcome seniors. Smartphones out of sight, please. Alright, you can call me Mr. Praetis, pronounced pray-tiss, like if someone combined Praying Mantis into one word. Weird, right? Senior year is a doozy, I get it. I’m sure you’re all ready to be done with grade school, but I hope that this final social studies class will teach you as much about history as it will about yourself. Yeah, you. That tired thing staring back in the mirror when you’re brushing your teeth. “But wait,” you’re thinking, “how can a boring old history class teach me about myself?” Consider this… we aren’t so different from the people who lived across the world thousands of years ago. They were intelligent like us. Felt fear like us. Felt love like us. They had complex thoughts and dreams. Some of them were influencers too, believe it or not, evolving the arts, tastes, and definitions of beauty. Their base perceptions are extremely similar to our own. And if we choose to believe that all of us in this world are actually more alike than we are different, then history is no longer random facts, but a look into who we are and where we can go. In this class, we're looking back to see ahead. What I’m handing out are copies of a letter from a local archaeologist called Quentin P. Brown. It was published in our local newspaper a long time ago. Even before I was born. My dad showed it to me and it made me want to teach social studies and eventually run for mayor. I talk about this piece so much that my poor kids at home have nearly memorized this thing. And I'm dorky enough to come up to come up with a rhyme that sums up the piece: "In the past we are found, sayeth Quentin P. Brown.” Now, who wants to read first?
target: 丹尼：歡迎，歡迎各位高年級同學。請把智慧型手機收起來。 好，你們可以叫我普雷蒂斯老師，念作 pray-tiss，就像把 Praying Mantis，也就是螳螂，合成一個字。很怪，對吧？ 最後一年不好熬，我懂。我相信各位都巴不得趕快告別中小學，但希望這最後一堂社會科，教你們認識歷史的同時，也能讓你們認識自己。對，就是你。你刷牙時，鏡子裡回望你的那個疲倦傢伙。 你們心裡一定想：「等等，一堂無聊的歷史課，怎麼會讓我認識自己？」想想看……我們和幾千年前住在世界各地的人，其實沒有那麼不同。 他們和我們一樣聰明，一樣會害怕，一樣會愛。他們有複雜的思想和夢想。信不信由你，其中有些人也是意見領袖，推動藝術、品味和美的定義。他們最基本的感受方式，和我們極為相似。如果我們願意相信，這個世界上的人，共通之處其實比差異更多，歷史就不再是一堆零散的事實，而是讓我們看見自己是誰、能往哪裡去。在這堂課，我們回望過去，是為了看清前路。 我現在發下去的，是本地一位考古學家昆汀・P・布朗寫的信。很久以前，它刊登在本地報紙上，甚至比我出生還早。我爸拿給我看後，讓我想成為社會科老師，最後甚至想競選鎮長。 我老是提這篇文章，家裡可憐的孩子們幾乎都會背了。我還書呆子到替它編了一句押韻的總結：「布朗說得好，過去把我們找到。」 好，誰想先讀？
